title: Atlas Health - Technical Deep Dive: Autoscaling & Capacity Planning
summary: Deep technical session on autoscaling strategies for LLM inference in a regulated healthcare environment. Discussed burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPU sizing, pre-warming, KV cache hit-rate implications, batching/windowing trade-offs, quantization impact on throughput, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run benchmark with Atlas sample workload, share capacity model spreadsheet, and provide security docs for private deployment.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-30 15:00 UTC | Duration 54 minutes | Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Atlas Head of ML), Samir Patel (Atlas Infra), Jenna Lopez (Atlas CISO), Ethan Brown (Product)

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick agenda: autoscaling & capacity planning for your pilot and eventual private deployment. Marcus will deep dive on the runtime implications.
[00:18] Priya: thanks Lena. our primary concerns are latency SLOs (95p < 300ms for short responses), predictable cost, and keeping data in our VPC. we also want to understand burst handling — our traffic spikes during morning sync and appointment booking windows.
[00:32] Marcus: yup, got it. quick overview — autoscaling levers: reserved GPU pool for steady state, pre-warmed burst pool for short spikes, and queueing + backpressure to protect latency SLOs. tradeoffs are cost vs tail latency.
[00:50] Samir: when you say pre-warmed, do you mean reserved but idle vms, or like hot containers with warmed KV cache?
[01:02] Marcus: both approaches exist. a pre-warmed GPU is literally reserved capacity so scheduling time is near zero; warm containers with KV cache pre-populated reduce first-token latency since KV cache fill is a big part of warmup for long-context models. but pre-populating cache has consistency concerns if prompts differ.
[01:24] Jenna: from security perspective, reserved GPUs in our VPC are preferred — can we get audit logs and KMS integration?
[01:32] Lena: yes — Private deployment supports KMS/HSM, audit logs, and RBAC. we'll send the redacted security package after this call.
[01:40] Ethan: curious about queueing models — are you modeling spikes with M/M/c or something more complex?
[01:48] Marcus: historically we start with an M/M/c approximation to estimate average queue length and wait times; then we simulate using actual arrival distributions (peaky, heavy tails) — results often deviate. For LLM inference, the service time distribution is not exponential because of variable sequence lengths, caching, and batching. so we run trace-driven sims.
[02:10] Priya: can you walk us through how batching window affects latency? we need 95p under 300ms for sub-100-token requests.
[02:21] Marcus: sure. batching increases throughput but adds batching delay. typical windowing approaches: fixed micro-batch windows (e.g., 10-20ms) or adaptive batching that flushes when either batch size or timeout threshold met. For your short requests, keep window tight (~5-12ms) and rely on continuous batching to collect small batches without hurting latency. Also, prefix KV cache can bypass some compute, reducing per-request service time.
[02:48] Samir: what's KV cache hit-rate impact? if cache hit-rate is low due to diverse prompts, does batching still help?
[02:56] Marcus: good question. KV cache helps most for conversational/reprompt scenarios where prefixes repeat. If hit-rate low, service times are longer and more variable, so batching helps amortize kernel launch costs but you get less benefit from cache. In simulations, cache hit-rate change from 20% to 60% can reduce GPU token compute by ~25-40% depending on model.
[03:20] Priya: do you have real numbers for reserved GPU sizing? say we expect sustained 250 qps of short prompts, average 60 tokens output.
[03:30] Marcus: ballpark — using a 13B-ish model quantized to int8 on an A100-class equivalent, one GPU can handle roughly 12-18 qps for short-turn workloads with small batch sizes if you maintain low latency (95p <300ms). So for 250 qps sustained you'd need ~14-22 GPUs reserved, plus a small pre-warm pool for bursts; numbers change with model size, quantization, and batching. We'll produce a spreadsheet with scenario columns.
[03:58] Jenna: any difference if we go H100 or mixed precision?
[04:04] Marcus: H100 improves throughput, you might get 1.6-2x depending on kernel efficiency and sequence length. Mixed precision (fp16) gives better perf than int8 in some runtimes for certain ops; but int8 quant gives huge memory savings for larger models enabling larger batch sizes. There's a tradeoff in quality and kernel support. We recommend benchmark runs on your sample set — we'll run those.
[04:29] Samir: how does autoscaler decide when to spin up GPUs? cold boot time for a new GPU pod is like multiple minutes in some clouds — unacceptable for short bursts.
[04:39] Marcus: exactly. that's why Redwood supports two-tier autoscaling: slow horizontal scale for steady growth (minutes) and fast burst pools using reserved idle instances or instant-warm containers. The burst policy can be time-limited and capped. We also support queue prioritization — critical requests can skip long queues and use burst capacity.
[05:01] Priya: is there a queuing timeout or shedding policy to avoid blowups? we can't let user-facing flows hit huge delays.
[05:08] Marcus: yes, you can set request-level SLOs and timeouts; beyond a threshold requests are either rejected or downgraded to a smaller model variant. Redwood's routing engine can fallback to cheaper/smaller models or cached responses if latency budgets exceeded.
[05:24] Ethan: downgrading sounds risky for quality-sensitive tasks like medical suggestions.
[05:29] Marcus: agreed — fallback should be used carefully. For clinical-critical flows, use dedicated reserved pool only. For non-critical assistant flows, fallback is a cost-safety net. You can mark routes as "no-fallback" in the config.
[05:44] Lena: just to align — Priya, which routes are hard SLOs vs best-effort?
[05:49] Priya: triage and appointment booking are hard SLOs; note generation and summarization are best-effort. We'll annotate routes in the prompts doc we send.
[05:58] Marcus: perfect. moving on: modeling burstiness. We typically ingest your request traces to compute peak-to-median ratios and run stress sims. Example: a 10x morning spike for 90s requires significantly more burst capacity than a sustained 2x.
[06:15] Samir: for pre-warm pools, do you keep KV cache warm across tenants? multi-tenant sharing is a no for us.
[06:22] Marcus: in Private deployments, pre-warms are tenant-isolated. For hosted mode, we do cost-sharing patterns but you can opt out. Pre-warm instances can be prepared with your common prefixes if you provide representative prompts.
[06:36] Jenna: about audit and telemetry: we need token-level latency breakdown and per-request logs for compliance. Can we retain logs on-prem?
[06:45] Lena: yes — with Private you control log retention and storage. We'll send the compliance package.
[06:51] Marcus: another point — batching windows and quantization: smaller quantized models run faster per token but may affect quality. If you can tolerate small quality delta, int8 enables larger batch sizes, which in turn improves throughput and reduces required GPUs. There's a compounding effect.
[07:11] Priya: can you quantify the compounding effect? an example scenario would help.
[07:16] Marcus: quick example — baseline fp16 per-GPU qps=15. int8 with stable kernels raises qps to 22 (approx 1.46x). If batching changes from average batch size 4 to 8 due to higher memory efficiency, you get another ~1.5x effective throughput, so combined you might see ~2.2x fewer GPUs needed. But numbers vary by model and kernel maturity.
[07:41] Samir: what's the overhead for KV cache replication across availability zones in VPC? we need HA.
[07:50] Marcus: KV cache is typically local to the serving node for latency. For HA you can warm adjacent nodes via periodic syncs but that adds network cost. Another approach is sticky routing of users to preferred node pools to improve cache locality.
[08:05] Priya: sticky routing might be ok for conversational agents but not for load-balanced booking APIs.
[08:11] Marcus: agreed. for stateless booking flows caching is less useful; focus on batching and reserved capacity.
[08:19] Ethan: what about queue metrics we should monitor to decide threshold tuning?
[08:24] Marcus: monitor queue depth, head-of-line wait time, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, kv-hit-rate, 95/99 latency, and pre-warm pool occupancy. We also expose per-model kernel saturation metrics.
[08:37] Priya: you mentioned kernel selection earlier — can Redwood switch kernels at runtime based on sequence length?
[08:44] Marcus: yes — the runtime can choose different execution paths for short vs long sequences, different attention kernels, or split runs across smaller micro-batches for long contexts. That helps keep latency predictable for short requests even when some requests are long.
[08:58] Samir: curious about admission control: do you implement token budget queues or request-level budgets?
[09:05] Marcus: we do both. token-budgeting prevents long-generation jobs from starving short ones. You can configure per-route/tenant token budgets and priority queues.
[09:13] Jenna: any examples of failure modes you've seen with autoscalers?
[09:18] Marcus: yes — typical issues: relying solely on CPU metrics to scale GPUs, slow cold starts, cache-thrashing due to poor routing, and not accounting for kernel variance at different sequence lengths. Those lead to oscillation or SLO breaches.
[09:33] Priya: what's Redwood's recommended safety margins? overprovision by 10-25%?
[09:39] Marcus: recommended steady-state buffer 10-20% plus a small pre-warm reserve sized by expected max spike magnitude and duration. For 10x short spikes, you need a pre-warm size equal to the incremental required GPUs for the spike's duration. If spikes are very short (<60s), we prefer pre-warmed instances; if they last minutes, you can rely on slow autoscale too.
[09:58] Ethan: can we keep a small hot pool only during business hours?
[10:02] Marcus: yes — schedule-based policies are supported. You can also combine with predictive scaling using historical patterns.
[10:09] Priya: what's the billing implication for pre-warmed reserved GPUs? flat monthly vs usage?
[10:15] Lena: Dedicated/reserved capacity is typically billed as a commit (monthly). Burst pools can be configured as reserved or on-demand with different price profiles. We'll put scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[10:24] Samir: network egress and data residency — if we use Private in our VPC, is traffic fully internal?
[10:30] Marcus: yes — Private deployment runs in your VPC/on-prem; traffic stays internal, and you control gateways.
[10:36] Jenna: what's onboarding time for on-prem? we've got extra security reviews.
[10:40] Lena: typical private on-prem engagements are 6-10 weeks (including compliance, infra prep, and validation). For VPC-private it's faster — 3-6 weeks depending on approvals.
[10:49] Marcus: returning to queue models — we'll run both analytic queue approximations and event-driven simulators using your traces. We'll show headroom curves and a suggested pre-warm sizing.
[10:59] Priya: can we also test with a smaller model fallback that preserves PII stripping? that's a regulatory requirement sometimes.
[11:07] Marcus: yes — we can test fallback to a smaller model for PII extraction flows; for anything clinical we recommend no fallback.
[11:14] Ethan: about observability — can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route?
[11:19] Lena: Redwood Console provides per-route token/latency/cost breakdowns and tracing hooks. We'll show the demo in the follow-up.
[11:26] Samir: when you run the benchmark, can you simulate our concurrency pattern (10s spikes, 5min windows)?
[11:31] Marcus: yes — please provide the sample distribution and a short script or traces; we'll replay with variable arrival patterns and show p99 latency, queue depth over time, and GPU utilization heatmaps.
[11:42] Priya: schedule-wise, if the benchmark looks good, how fast can we pilot?
[11:47] Lena: we can spin up a pilot on Redwood Dedicated in 2-3 weeks after sign-off, or quicker for hosted API (self-serve) but given data residency you'll likely go Dedicated or Private.
[11:58] Jenna: do you support customer-managed KMS in Dedicated?
[12:02] Marcus: yes, we integrate with AWS KMS and common HSMs.
[12:06] Priya: any gotchas about KV cache and encryption in-transit?
[12:11] Marcus: KV cache lives encrypted at rest and in transit; for on-prem customers you can apply additional disk-level encryption policies. Some runtimes require in-memory keys for performance; we document those tradeoffs.
[12:24] Ethan: it'd be helpful to see a worked example: given 250 qps sustained with 10x 90-second spikes, what's the recommended config?
[12:33] Marcus: rough walkthrough: steady-state reserved GPUs for 250 qps — as I said earlier ~14-22 GPUs depending on model. For spikes, either add a pre-warm pool sized to handle the delta to peak — if peak is 2500 qps that's +~140-180 GPUs; obviously cost-prohibitive so we recommend capacity shaping: (1) route non-critical traffic to queued/bulk path, (2) use smaller/faster models for spikes, (3) use rate-limits or progressive degradation for extremes. The spreadsheet will show cost tradeoffs per option.
[13:08] Priya: that delta seems large — if we can accept slightly higher 95p (e.g., 400ms) during spikes does that reduce GPUs a lot?
[13:17] Marcus: yes, relaxing latency SLO allows larger batching and more time to autoscale, which can drastically reduce required burst capacity. There's a nonlinear relationship.
[13:24] Samir: any internal throttling primitives to enforce per-tenant budgets?
[13:29] Marcus: yes, token budgets and quota gates are plumbed into the routing layer. You can also set per-route caps that trigger graceful degradation.
[13:36] Lena: quick check — Jenna, any more security blockers for proceeding to benchmark?
[13:41] Jenna: need to review SOC2 artifacts and encryption details; if those look ok we'll proceed. Please send docs.
[13:48] Lena: will do. Marcus, anything else we should include in the benchmark?
[13:52] Marcus: include tests for: varying sequence lengths, prefix-repeat scenarios to measure KV-hit benefits, cold-start tests for scale-up latency, and quantization quality checks.
[14:02] Priya: can Redwood run A/B between fp16 and int8 on our prompts?
[14:07] Marcus: yes — we'll produce side-by-side latency, throughput, and quality diff metrics.
[14:12] Ethan: what's the expected variance between cloud providers? we're leaning multi-cloud for redundancy.
[14:18] Marcus: underlying NICs, GPU generation, and kernel stacks make measurable differences. H100 on GCP vs A100 on AWS will show different perf; we can run cross-cloud benchmarks but note networking costs.
[14:28] Priya: final question — for on-prem, what's the recommended GPU mix for a balanced pilot?
[14:34] Marcus: start with homogeneous GPUs (e.g., A100 80GB or similar) to simplify kernel selection. If you need variety for cost reasons, we can profile and create instance-type aware routing.
[14:45] Samir: thanks. any docs you can share summarizing these recommendations?
[14:49] Lena: we'll send the capacity model spreadsheet, security package, and a runbook for the benchmark.
[14:55] Marcus: ok I'll note the benchmark config.
[15:00] Priya: thanks everyone — looks productive.

[End of transcript — roughly 54 minutes; occasional speaker labeling may be approximate due to auto-transcription.]
